title: Google wants to let you use your phone as a remote Googlebook trackpad
summary: Remote Googlebook control could be possible with a "Cast trackpad" on Android phones.
body: TL;DR Googlebook laptops are arriving soon, featuring heavy cross-connectivity with Android phones. Users will be able to cast apps from phones to their Googlebook in order to remotely interact with them. It now appears that we’ll also be able to control Googlebooks remotely by using phone touchscreens as a trackpad. Do you ever think of your phone as a remote control? We already use our phones to control countless other devices through the apps they connect to, but somehow that feels like a different class of interaction entirely. Maybe the closest example of employing a phone as a straight-up remote is something like the Google TV control offered through that app and Google Home, letting us operate smart TVs with a phone’s touchscreen. And now we’re getting an early look at where Google could be trying this same sort of approach next. You’re reading an Authority Insights story. title: Google’s new Gemini feature aimed at multitaskers is starting to roll out
summary: Google quietly begins its gradual roll out of the Gemini overlay’s new minimize UI.
body: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority TL;DR Google has been working on adding the ability to minimize the Gemini overlay. Users are now starting to see the option on their devices. It appears Google is gradually rolling out the new button. While it’s not necessarily a problem, the Gemini overlay taking over the screen isn’t exactly ideal for multitaskers. Since it locks you in, you can’t really do anything else on your phone until you’re done with the chatbot. Last year, we spotted evidence that Google was working on fixing this oversight with a minimize function. Now it appears Google has started rolling out its solution. Users are reporting ( 1 , 2 , 3 ) that they are starting to see a new minimize button for the Gemini overlay. Based on the examples, the UI looks similar to the design we discovered in June , which adds a dedicated “Minimize Gemini” button that stays visible throughout your conversation with the AI. In the first version we saw, there was no button, which could have kept a lot of users from discovering the option.

title: Your older Pixel phone may finally be getting Quick Share AirDrop support
summary: Pixel 7 and Pixel 8 users are starting to see surprise AirDrop alerts.
body: TL;DR Android picked up cross-platform Quick Share/AirDrop support last fall, but access has been limited to specific device models. On the Pixel front, that’s included phones from the Pixel 8a on up, but earlier today we learned of a possible expansion to the Pixel Tablet. We’re now also getting reports of Pixel 7 and Pixel 8 users seeing notifications of this new support. Devices that won’t play nicely together suck . Sometimes incompatibility is the design goal, trying to lock you into one ecosystem or another. Other times it’s a glitch, or even just developer callousness. But however it starts, we’re always glad to see it come to an end. Android and iOS devices have been inching closer towards peaceful co-existence with the arrival of cross AirDrop/Quick Share support , and now it looks like a long-overdue expansion is taking place. Google started bringing AirDrop compatibility to Quick Share on Pixel 10 phones last fall, eventually expanding that down through the Pixel 8a series . And while that list now also includes the new Pixel 11 family, we’ve been wondering when the rest of the Pixel crew might be invited to join the party.

summary: The nearly 30-year-old service expands to vehicle screens to maintain its viral app store momentum.
body: Credit: IGameShit / Reddit TL;DR MapQuest has launched experimental Android Auto support, bringing its mapping service directly to vehicle dashboards. body: It’s usually difficult to get excited about a new Android browser . Unlike the launcher space, which includes a puzzle piece for almost every conceivable niche, browsers are mostly limited to two major schools of thought: you can go with a browser based on Firefox ’s underpinnings, or one based on Chromium, the underlying technology that powers Google Chrome. Since these platforms on which browsers are built are largely immutable, any new browser release must innovate in other core areas that matter — aesthetics, usability, and customizability.

While WHOOP has long dominated the screenless fitness tracker world, that dominance has recently been shaken by the emergence of Google’s Fitbit Air and Garmin’s CIRQA Smart Band . However, those two aren’t the only challengers WHOOP may need to be concerned about, as smart ring maker Luna revealed its intentions to enter the market earlier this year. If you’ve been waiting to get a Luna Band, you won’t have to wait much longer. Months after the Luna Band made its debut at CES, Luna announced in May that the waitlist for the wearable was open. Pre-orders started on July 4, and the first shipments were scheduled for July 31. Back at Google I/O, the company showed how Gemini could make Gmail, Docs, and Keep feel less like apps you operate and more like assistants you talk to. The company promised that these new voice-powered experiences would be available this summer, and after a few early glimpses , the wait is finally over. Gmail Live, Docs Live, and Keep Live are rolling out now, giving users new ways to get things done without reaching for the keyboard. Gmail Live is perhaps the most immediately useful of the three. Instead of digging through your inbox or remembering the right keywords, you can ask a question out loud. Gmail can connect information across emails to synthesize an answer.
